title: Container With Most Water — opposite-end, move shorter side.
shortTitle: Container With Most Water — Opposite-End, Move the Shorter Side

s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Container With Most Water takes an array of heights representing vertical lines and finds two lines that, with the x-axis, form a container holding the most water. The area between two lines is the smaller of the two heights multiplied by the distance between them. Opposite-end two pointers start at both ends and repeatedly move the pointer at the shorter line inward, tracking the maximum area, in O(n) time and O(1) space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of each bar as the balance on a day, and we want the widest, deepest "reserve pool" we can form between two days. The water level is capped by the shorter of the two day-balances, and the width is the number of days between them. Rajesh starts with the first and last day, keeps whichever is taller, and moves the shorter day inward hoping to find a taller wall that holds more.

**One line to remember:** Water is limited by the shorter wall, so moving the shorter pointer inward is the only move that can possibly increase the area.

sections.s2_technical:
Set `left = 0` and `right = n - 1`. The area for the current pair is `Math.min(h[left], h[right]) * (right - left)`. You record the maximum area seen so far, then move inward. The key decision: move the pointer at the shorter line. If `h[left] < h[right]` move `left++`, else move `right--`.

Why move the shorter side? The area is bounded by the shorter line. If you move the taller line inward, the width shrinks and the height is still capped by the unchanged shorter line, so the area cannot increase. Moving the shorter line is the only move that gives a chance at a taller limiting wall that could overcome the lost width. This greedy argument is the core of the solution.

A code snippet on day balances: `int maxArea(int[] h) { int l = 0, r = h.length - 1, best = 0; while (l < r) { int area = Math.min(h[l], h[r]) * (r - l); best = Math.max(best, area); if (h[l] < h[r]) l++; else r--; } return best; }`. Each step moves one pointer, they never cross back, so it is linear.

A senior nuance is why the greedy does not miss a better pair: when we discard the shorter line, every pair that still includes that shorter line as the limiting wall would have had width no larger than the current one, so none of them can beat what we already considered; discarding it loses nothing. When the two heights are equal, moving either side is fine because both would be limited identically. The brute-force alternative compares every pair in O(n squared), which the two-pointer approach reduces to O(n).
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India treasury models a liquidity window as two days, where the usable reserve between them is capped by the lower end-of-day balance times the number of days in the window. The treasury wants the window that maximizes this product. This is exactly how Container With Most Water works — the limiting height is the smaller balance and the width is the day gap.

Problem 2 — There can be thousands of days, so an all-pairs scan is too slow for an interactive dashboard, which is why the linear two-pointer approach matters.

The code shows a `LiquidityWindowAnalyzer` with `maxReserve`, a demo on a series of daily balances, and the best window's reserve value.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: balances [1, 8, 6, 2, 5, 4, 8, 3, 7], indexes 0 to 8.

Step 1: `left` at index 0 (height 1), `right` at index 8 (height 7). The limiting height is 1, width is 8, area is 8. Best is 8. Since the left wall is shorter, move `left` to index 1.

Step 2: `left` at index 1 (height 8), `right` at index 8 (height 7). Limiting height 7, width 7, area 49. Best is now 49. The right wall is shorter, so move `right` to index 7.

Step 3: `left` 8, `right` index 7 (height 3). Height 3, width 6, area 18, not better. Move `right` to index 6 (height 8). Height 8, width 5, area 40, not better. Move `right` (equal heights, move right) to index 5 (height 4). Area is 4 times 4 equals 16.

Step 4: Continuing, every remaining pair yields an area below 49 because the width keeps shrinking faster than the height can grow. The best stays 49.

Step 5: The loop ends when the pointers meet, and the method returns 49 as the maximum reserve window value.

```

```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Container With Most Water asks me to pick two vertical lines from an array of heights so that the container they form with the ground holds the most water, where the water volume is the shorter of the two heights multiplied by the horizontal distance between them. I solve it with opposite-end two pointers starting at the first and last lines. At each step I compute the current area, update my running maximum, and then move the pointer sitting on the shorter line inward.

The reason I always move the shorter side is the heart of the solution. The area is capped by the shorter line, so if I moved the taller line inward the width would shrink while the height stayed limited by the same short line, and the area could never improve. Moving the shorter line is the only move that gives a chance at a taller limiting wall that might more than make up for the lost width. When the two heights are equal, moving either side is fine because both are limited the same way.

The subtle guarantee is that discarding the shorter line never loses a better answer, because any other pair that still used that short line as its limit would have had a width no larger than the one I just evaluated, so it could not beat what I already recorded. That is why the greedy pass is correct and I do not need the brute-force comparison of every pair, which would be quadratic.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this shape of problem in the treasury dashboard to find the liquidity window between two days whose usable reserve, capped by the lower end-of-day balance and scaled by the number of days, was largest. With thousands of days an all-pairs scan was far too slow for an interactive dashboard, so the linear two-pointer approach made it responsive. Explaining the area formula, the move-the-shorter-wall rule, and why discarding the shorter line is safe shows the interviewer I understand the greedy reasoning rather than just the code.
